alt.en: A printed book page headed "The folk-song of the Ashkenazim", page 401, "Table XXXII, Tunes of the Eastern Ashkenazic folk-song". Tune No. 1, marked Moderato, is a single line of melody with the words "E-li-yo-hu ha-no-vi, e-li-yo-hu ha-tish-bi" under it, a Fine sign, and a line marked recitando. Below are tune No. 2, marked recit., on "E-li-yo-hu ha-no-vi", and tune No. 3, "Ha-mav-dil ben ko-desh le-chol".
alt.es: Página impresa de un libro con el encabezado "The folk-song of the Ashkenazim", página 401, "Table XXXII, Tunes of the Eastern Ashkenazic folk-song". La melodía n.º 1, marcada Moderato, es una sola línea melódica con la letra "E-li-yo-hu ha-no-vi, e-li-yo-hu ha-tish-bi" debajo, un signo de Fine y una línea marcada recitando. Debajo están la melodía n.º 2, marcada recit., sobre "E-li-yo-hu ha-no-vi", y la n.º 3, "Ha-mav-dil ben ko-desh le-chol".

caption.en: Page 401 of A. Z. Idelsohn's Jewish Music in its Historical Development (1929): No. 1 in Table XXXII, "Tunes of the Eastern Ashkenazic folk-song", is the tune we sing, with the words spelled the Ashkenazi way, "Eliyohu hanovi".
caption.es: La página 401 de Jewish Music in its Historical Development (1929), de A. Z. Idelsohn: el n.º 1 de la tabla XXXII, "Tunes of the Eastern Ashkenazic folk-song", es la melodía que cantamos, con la letra escrita a la manera asquenazí, "Eliyohu hanovi".

source: A. Z. Idelsohn, Jewish Music in its Historical Development (copyright 1929 by Henry Holt and Company; this copy a Tudor Publishing Company printing from the same pages), p. 401, Table XXXII, Nos. 1 to 3
library: Princeton Theological Seminary Library (digitized by the Internet Archive)
licenceEvidence: Copyright 1929 (title-page verso: "Copyright, 1929, by Henry Holt and Company, Inc."), so public domain in the US since 1 January 2025; A. Z. Idelsohn died 1938 (LoC name authority "1882-1938"), so life plus 70 ended in 2008 in the EU and Israel; the tunes are traditional (see rights.md).
credit: Princeton Theological Seminary Library, via the Internet Archive

alt.en: Two paragraphs of printed English text beginning "The Cup of Elijah." in small capitals: "The fifth promise of God (V'hevesi) to bring Israel into Canaan, which follows the four promises of redemption, gave rise to the question of the need of a fifth cup of wine in the Seder." The second paragraph says the fifth cup came to be known as the Cup of Elijah and gave rise to the custom of opening the door.
alt.es: Dos párrafos de texto impreso en inglés que empiezan con "The Cup of Elijah." en versalitas: "The fifth promise of God (V'hevesi) to bring Israel into Canaan, which follows the four promises of redemption, gave rise to the question of the need of a fifth cup of wine in the Seder." El segundo párrafo dice que la quinta copa llegó a llamarse la copa de Elías y dio origen a la costumbre de abrir la puerta.

caption.en: "The Cup of Elijah", from the introduction to The Union Haggadah (Central Conference of American Rabbis, 1923), which traces Elijah's cup to the question of a fifth cup of wine at the seder, a question left for Elijah to settle.
caption.es: "The Cup of Elijah" (la copa de Elías), de la introducción de The Union Haggadah (Central Conference of American Rabbis, 1923), que remonta la copa de Elías a la duda sobre una quinta copa de vino en el séder, una duda que se dejó para que Elías la resolviera.

source: The Union Haggadah: Home Service for the Passover, revised edition, edited and published by the Central Conference of American Rabbis (copyright 1923), introduction, "Rites and Symbols of the Seder", p. xii, "The Cup of Elijah"
library: University of Florida, George A. Smathers Libraries (digitized by the Internet Archive)
callNumber: Internet Archive unionhaggadahhom00unse; UF catalog UF000858031
licenceEvidence: Title-page verso: "Edited and published by the Central Conference of American Rabbis. Copyright 1923", so public domain in the US (published before 1931); the IA record: "Copyright status reviewed by UF staff - Out of copyright". The introduction is unsigned, a corporate work, so 70 years from publication ended in 1993 in the EU and Israel (see rights.md).
credit: University of Florida, George A. Smathers Libraries, via the Internet Archive

alt.en: A black-and-white photograph of a tall silver spice box shaped like a castle tower: a pointed, scaled spire over a round turret with two small windows, a gallery with little corner turrets, a square body of engraved brickwork with a clock face and a small arched door, all on a flared base.
alt.es: Fotografía en blanco y negro de una caja de especias de plata alta, con forma de torre de castillo: una aguja puntiaguda de escamas sobre un torreón redondo con dos ventanitas, una galería con torrecillas en las esquinas, un cuerpo cuadrado de ladrillos grabados con una esfera de reloj y una puertecita en arco, todo sobre una base acampanada.

caption.en: A silver spice box in the form of a tower, thought to have been made in Laupheim, Germany, about 1740, as the US National Museum photographed it for a 1929 bulletin; Havdalah is said over wine, spices and a flame, and Eliyahu HaNavi is sung after it.
caption.es: Una caja de especias de plata en forma de torre, que se cree hecha en Laupheim (Alemania) hacia 1740, tal como la fotografió el Museo Nacional de Estados Unidos para un boletín de 1929; la Havdalá se dice sobre el vino, las especias y una llama, y después se canta Eliyahu HaNavi.

source: Immanuel Moses Casanowicz, Collections of Objects of Religious Ceremonial in the United States National Museum, Bulletin 148 (Washington: Government Printing Office, 1929), Plate 3 (lower), fig. 4; described on p. 9, No. 25, "Silver spice box"
library: Smithsonian Libraries (digitized by the Internet Archive)
callNumber: U.S.N.M. Cat. No. 130297; Internet Archive bulletinunitedst1481929unit
licenceEvidence: Printed by the US Government Printing Office, 1929, so public domain in the US (published before 1931; also a federal museum publication); the IA record: "Not in copyright." Author Casanowicz died 26 September 1927 (the bulletin's own note); the museum photographer is not named. PD in the EU and Israel (see rights.md).
